blocks.text:
Design the core engine behind a logging framework (the kind that powers Log4j or SLF4J style logging). The distinguishing challenge is two-tier, independent level filtering: a logger has its own overall threshold that can drop a message before anyone else even sees it, and every destination the message could go to, an appender, has its own separate threshold on top of that, letting one appender capture everything while another shows only the important parts.

  • Actors: Application code (calls the logger), LoggerFactory (creates and caches named loggers).
  • Scope: log levels, two-tier threshold filtering, pluggable formatting and output destinations, and name-based logger caching.

The distinguishing mechanic is a real two-gate filtering pipeline: the logger's own threshold decides whether a message is even worth producing at all, and each appender's own threshold independently decides whether that specific destination cares about it, combined with a factory that always returns the identical logger instance for a given name.
The system must support the following core capabilities:

items: Get a named logger: repeated lookups for the same name must return the identical logger instance.
Log a message at a level: DEBUG, INFO, WARN, or ERROR, filtered first by the logger's own threshold.
Register multiple appenders: each with its own independent minimum level and its own output format.
Format log output: support at least plain text and JSON formatting, chosen per appender.
Reject invalid configuration: a blank logger name, a duplicate appender registration, or removing an appender that was never added.

blocks.text: Beyond correctness, the design should hold up along five quality pillars:

metadata.alt: Five non-functional pillars: scalability, extensibility, maintainability, performance, thread safety

items: Scalability: a large codebase with many named loggers must not require touching existing logging logic.
Extensibility: a new appender destination or a new output format should plug in without rewriting the logger.
Maintainability: formatting, output, and instance lookup are isolated in their own classes.
Performance: a message dropped below the logger's own threshold costs a single comparison, never touching any appender.
Thread safety: concurrent logging from many threads, and concurrent lookups of the same new logger name, must both behave correctly.

blocks.text: Questions worth asking the interviewer before designing:

items: Should a logger's threshold be configurable at runtime, or fixed at creation time?
Should child loggers inherit configuration from a parent logger by name hierarchy, as many real frameworks do?
Is asynchronous, buffered writing required, or is synchronous, immediate writing acceptable?
Should log records include structured contextual fields beyond the message string?
Is log rotation or retention in scope, or purely the logging call path itself?

blocks.text: To keep the design focused, we make these explicit assumptions:

items: Logger thresholds are set at creation time and can be reconfigured directly on the instance, but there is no parent-child hierarchy in this design.
Logging is synchronous, a log call blocks until every registered appender has processed the message.
The file appender simulates file output by accumulating formatted lines in memory, representing what would otherwise be written to disk.
A log record carries only a sequence number, logger name, level, and message, no structured contextual fields.
Log rotation and retention policies are out of scope, noted as a follow-up.

blocks.text: The design centers on four core entities:

metadata.alt: Core entities: Logger, LogAppender, LogFormatter, and LogRecord

items: Logger: a named source of log events with its own threshold and a set of registered appenders.
LogAppender: one output destination, with its own threshold and its own formatter.
LogFormatter: converts a log record into an output string.
LogRecord: one logged event, capturing its level, source logger, and message.

blocks.text: These entities connect through a small set of well-defined relationships:

metadata.alt: A logger has many appenders; each appender formats through one formatter; a logger produces log records that are delivered to every appender

items: Logger to LogAppender is one-to-many.
LogAppender to LogFormatter is one-to-one, each appender owns its own formatting strategy.
Logger to LogRecord is a production relationship: every log call that passes the logger's threshold produces one record.

blocks.text: Three patterns keep formatting, output, and instance lookup decoupled from the core logger.
Why needed: plain text and JSON formatting fundamentally disagree on how a log record becomes a string, and different appenders legitimately want different formats for the same underlying record.

metadata.alt: LogFormatter interface with PlainTextLogFormatter and JsonLogFormatter implementations

blocks.text: Why it is the best fit: a new output format (XML, a custom structured format) is a new strategy implementation, with zero changes to Logger or any appender's filtering logic. What it solves: it isolates formatting rules from the shared, stable filtering and delivery algorithm.
Why needed: a single log event often needs to reach several independent destinations at once, each deciding for itself whether the event matters to it.

metadata.alt: LogAppender interface notified by Logger, each appender carrying its own threshold and formatter

blocks.text: Why it is the best fit: Logger does not need to know what an appender does with a record, only that it should be notified. What it solves: it decouples the core filtering workflow from output side effects.
Why needed: every part of a codebase that logs under the same name should share configuration and behavior, which only works if they all share the exact same Logger instance.

metadata.alt: LoggerFactory caching Logger instances by name, returning the same instance on repeated lookups

blocks.text: Why it is the best fit: callers never construct a Logger directly, so the factory is the single place identity and configuration are controlled. What it solves: this is a common real-world variant of the Factory pattern, one that additionally caches and returns existing instances rather than always constructing a fresh one.
Each class has a single, clear responsibility:

items: Logger: attributes name, minLevel, appenders; responsibility: gate log calls against its own threshold and notify appenders.
LogAppender implementations: attributes minLevel, formatter; responsibility: independently gate and write a record to one destination.
LogFormatter implementations: responsibility: render one record into an output string.
LoggerFactory: attributes a name-to-instance cache; responsibility: create and reuse named logger instances.

blocks.text: Two interfaces keep the design open for extension:

metadata.alt: LogFormatter and LogAppender interfaces with their key methods

items: LogFormatter: format(record): abstracts away exactly how a record becomes an output string.
LogAppender: onLog(record): abstracts away which destinations exist and how each independently decides to act.

blocks.text: Three flows below cover named logger caching, the two-tier filtering pipeline, and a rejected duplicate appender registration.

metadata.alt: Two lookups for the same logger name return the exact same cached instance
A DEBUG message is dropped by the logger's own threshold before any appender is notified; an INFO message passes the logger but is then independently accepted or ignored by each appender
Registering the same appender instance a second time on the same logger is rejected

blocks.text: The two-tier filtering workflow, alongside its rejection branch, looks like this:

metadata.alt: The logger's own threshold gates first; only messages that pass are offered to every appender, each of which applies its own independent threshold

items: Happy path, dropped early: log a message below the logger's own threshold → dropped immediately, no appender is ever notified.
Happy path, delivered selectively: log a message that passes the logger's threshold → every appender is notified → each writes it only if it also passes that appender's own, independent threshold.
Rejection path: register the same appender instance twice on one logger → rejected, since duplicate registration would produce duplicate output lines for every future message.

blocks.text: The service exposes a small, intention-revealing API:

items: LoggerFactory.getLogger(name): returns the cached logger for this name, creating one on first use.
Logger.log(level, message): gates against the logger's own threshold, then notifies every registered appender.
Logger.addAppender(appender): registers a new output destination, rejecting an already-registered instance.
Logger.removeAppender(appender): unregisters a destination, rejecting one that was never added.

blocks.text: Three custom exceptions cover the realistic failure modes:

items: InvalidLoggerNameException: getLogger is called with a blank or empty name.
DuplicateAppenderException: the same appender instance is registered on a logger a second time.
AppenderNotRegisteredException: removeAppender is called with an appender that was never added to that logger.

blocks.text: The critical race is two threads requesting the same brand-new logger name at nearly the same moment.

metadata.alt: Two threads racing to create a logger for the same new name; synchronization ensures one thread creates and caches it before the other reads the cache

blocks.text: Synchronizing the check-then-create step in the factory's cache ensures two concurrent lookups for a brand-new name can never both construct and cache a separate Logger, which would silently break the identity guarantee the whole design depends on.
The pattern choices make several future features low-friction to add:

items: A new output format (XML, a custom structured format) is a new LogFormatter implementation.
A new destination (a network log shipper, a database sink) is a new LogAppender implementation.
Parent-child logger hierarchies can be layered on by having a logger consult a parent's appenders when its own threshold passes.
Asynchronous, buffered writing can be added by wrapping any LogAppender in a queue-backed decorator without changing Logger at all.
Single Responsibility: Logger gates and delivers, LogFormatter renders, LogAppender writes, each for one reason to change.
Open/Closed: new formats or destinations extend via new classes, not edits to Logger.
Liskov Substitution: any LogFormatter or LogAppender implementation can replace another without breaking the logger.
Interface Segregation: LogAppender exposes only the single callback a destination actually needs.
Dependency Inversion: Logger depends on the LogAppender interface, and each appender depends on the LogFormatter interface, never on concrete classes.
A message exactly at the logger's threshold level is accepted, using an inclusive comparison, not just messages strictly above it.
An appender configured with a stricter threshold than the logger it is attached to simply never sees the messages the logger already lets through below that stricter line.
A logger with zero registered appenders still accepts and processes log calls that pass its own threshold, it simply has nobody to notify.
Two different logger names that happen to share a prefix are still entirely independent instances with independent thresholds and appenders.
log: O(1) if dropped by the logger's own threshold, otherwise O(a) where a is the number of registered appenders.
getLogger: O(1) amortized, a single cache lookup and, on a cache miss, a single insertion.
Space: O(loggers + appenders) held in memory.

blocks.text: A relational schema shows how logs and appender configuration could be persisted for a database-backed log store:

metadata.alt: ER diagram: Logger, LogRecord, and AppenderConfig

items: LOG_RECORD stores every accepted record, keyed by a monotonically increasing sequence number for stable ordering.
APPENDER_CONFIG lets a deployment's appender wiring be reconstructed from configuration rather than hardcoded at startup.
Add parent-child logger hierarchies with configuration inheritance.
Support asynchronous, buffered appenders for high-throughput logging.
Add structured contextual fields to LogRecord beyond a single message string.
In a distributed deployment, ship log records to a centralized aggregation service instead of, or alongside, local appenders.

codes.python:
from enum import Enum

# Severity of a single log record, ordered from least to most severe.
class LogLevel(Enum):
    DEBUG = 0
    INFO = 1
    WARN = 2
    ERROR = 3

# One logged event, capturing its origin, level, and message.
class LogRecord:
    def __init__(self, sequence_number, logger_name, level, message):
        self.sequence_number = sequence_number  # monotonically increasing order marker
        self.logger_name = logger_name            # which logger produced this record
        self.level = level                          # severity of this record
        self.message = message                        # the logged text

# Custom exceptions for the realistic failure modes.
class InvalidLoggerNameException(Exception): pass
class DuplicateAppenderException(Exception): pass
class AppenderNotRegisteredException(Exception): pass

items: Why filter at both the logger level and the appender level instead of just one? Because they solve different problems: the logger threshold controls how much work the application even bothers producing, while each appender's threshold controls how much of that production actually reaches a given destination, letting one appender capture everything for debugging while another shows only what operators need to see.

Why does LoggerFactory cache instances by name rather than construct a fresh Logger every time? Because two different parts of a codebase logging under the same name need to share configuration and see each other's appender wiring, which is only possible if they are working with the exact same object.

How would you extend this to support parent-child logger hierarchies? Give each Logger an optional parent reference, and have log delivery also walk up to parent loggers' appenders after the current logger's own, the same design real frameworks like Log4j use.

Two-tier filtering vs a single global threshold: two-tier filtering gives fine-grained control per destination, at the cost of slightly more configuration to reason about; a single global threshold is simpler but forces every destination to see exactly the same set of messages.

Synchronous logging vs asynchronous, buffered logging: synchronous logging is simple and guarantees a message is fully processed before the call returns, at the cost of coupling application latency to however slow the slowest appender is; asynchronous logging decouples that latency at the cost of added complexity and the risk of losing buffered messages on a crash.

Name-based caching vs constructing a Logger by hand each time: caching guarantees shared configuration and identity for a given name, at the cost of a small amount of synchronization overhead on lookup; manual construction avoids that overhead but risks two parts of a codebase silently drifting out of sync on the same logical logger.
Persist critical log configuration (which appenders exist, their thresholds) externally so it can be adjusted without redeploying, using the schema in the Database Design section as a starting point.
Replace the in-memory FileLogAppender simulation with real, rotated file output or a network log shipper in production.
Add asynchronous, buffered appenders for high-throughput services where synchronous logging would otherwise become a bottleneck.
Monitor dropped-message counts per logger to catch a threshold misconfiguration that is silently hiding important log output.
